transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well... I think what finally pushed me to come in is that I scared myself a little. I’ve been having these thoughts—not that I have a plan to do anything, I don’t—but thoughts like, “Maybe it would just be simpler if I didn’t wake up tomorrow.” And I know that’s not a good place for my mind to be going.

It’s hard to say out loud, honestly. I kept telling myself it was just a passing thought, that people probably have dark thoughts when they’re overwhelmed or tired, but it’s been enough that I thought, no, I should probably talk to someone before I pretend it’s nothing.
Has this low mood been present most days for at least two years?

No, not two years. It feels long, but it’s been more like… about eight months, I think. It really started after my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly. That’s when I noticed this heaviness settling in most days, and it just hasn’t really lifted the way I kept hoping it would.
Do you feel that your low mood is mainly a reaction to what happened with your brother?

I think so, yes… at least that’s when it really began. It’s hard for me to separate it, because before that I had normal ups and downs, of course, but this particular low mood — the one that’s been hanging around and not really letting up — it started around when my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly.

It’s been about eight months now. I kept thinking maybe I was just reacting to the shock of it, or adjusting, and that with time I’d feel more like myself again. But it’s gone on long enough that it doesn’t feel like just a bad week or a temporary reaction anymore. Still, if you’re asking what it’s tied to in my mind, yes, I do connect it very strongly to what happened with him.
During this period, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yes… yes, I have. I notice it most with my watercolor painting. I still go through the motions sometimes — I’ll take out the paints, set up the little cup of water, tape the paper down, all of that — but then I just sit there looking at the blank page.

It used to feel soothing, almost absorbing, choosing colors and watching the light come through them. Now it’s like I’m waiting for that feeling to show up, and it just… doesn’t. After a while I’ll put everything away again, feeling sort of foolish for even trying. It’s not that I’ve decided I don’t like painting anymore. It’s more like the pleasure part of it is missing.
Has this been making it hard for you to function in your daily life?

Yes, it has, though I wouldn’t say everything has fallen apart. I’m still managing the basics — I keep the house going, I get meals together, I pay the bills, that sort of thing. From the outside, someone might think I’m doing alright because the essentials are getting done.

But it’s changed the way I live my days. I used to go regularly with my walking group, and I’ve pulled back from that quite a bit. I’ll tell myself I’m going to go, I’ll even get my shoes by the door sometimes, and then I just… don’t follow through. And with mentoring, too — that used to mean a lot to me, being present for someone, listening carefully, encouraging them — but lately I don’t feel fully there with people. I find myself worrying that I’m not giving them what I used to.

So yes, it’s making daily life harder, just maybe in a quieter way. I’m functioning, but I’m not really participating the way I used to.
During this time, have you been feeling excessively worried or anxious?

I’m not sure I’d call it excessive worry, exactly. I mean, I do think about things — probably more than I used to — and I can get caught up in my head a bit, especially when I’m already feeling low. But when you say “anxious,” I’m not completely sure whether what I’m feeling fits that.

It’s more like a heaviness or a preoccupation than that keyed-up, panicky feeling I imagine when people talk about anxiety. I wouldn’t say I’m constantly worrying about lots of different things or feeling on edge all day. There are moments, certainly, but I haven’t really noticed anxiety as the main thing, if that makes sense.
Before this period began, have you ever had another episode in your life when you felt depressed like this for at least two weeks?

I’m not really sure. I’ve certainly had sad periods in my life, you know, times when things felt harder or I was discouraged for a while, but I’m having trouble sorting out whether any of those were truly like this and lasted at least two weeks in the same way.

I don’t want to say yes if I’m just remembering ordinary difficult times and stretching them into something more than they were. This feels particular enough that I’m not immediately thinking, “Oh yes, this happened before.” But I also don’t keep a perfect record of my moods, especially going back over many years. So… I suppose my honest answer is that I’m not sure. I can’t clearly identify another episode like this.
Do these feelings seem stronger than you would expect from what happened with your brother?

I don’t know… that’s a hard one for me to judge. Part of me thinks, well, he’s my brother, and what happened shook me, so of course I’d feel it deeply. I don’t want to make it sound as if there’s some “correct” amount of sadness I’m supposed to have, because family things don’t really work that way.

But then I also wonder if I’m not seeing it clearly from inside it. Some days I think, maybe this is just grief or strain doing what it does, and other days I think, why am I still feeling so weighed down by it in the way I am? I’m not sure whether that means it’s stronger than expected, or whether I just expected myself to cope differently.

So… I guess I can’t give you a clean yes or no. It feels connected to what happened with him, definitely, but whether it’s out of proportion, I honestly don’t know.
Looking back over your life, was there ever a time before these last eight months when you felt depressed or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I’m still not sure, honestly. I’ve been trying to think back carefully, because I don’t want to give you an answer that sounds more certain than I really feel.

There were definitely times in my life when I was unhappy, or disappointed, or going through something stressful, and I may have felt down for stretches. But when you say depressed or losing interest nearly every day for at least two weeks, I’m not able to clearly point to a specific earlier period and say, “Yes, that was the same kind of thing.” It all gets a bit blurry looking back, especially because I probably didn’t think about it in those terms at the time.

So I suppose my answer is… I don’t know. I can’t confidently say yes. If it happened, it isn’t something I can clearly remember or identify the way I can describe what’s been going on these past months.
During these past eight months, have you had trouble sleeping?

Yes, I have. Not every single night in exactly the same way, but it’s been enough that I notice it. I’ll go to bed tired, and sometimes I can fall asleep, but it’s uneven—some nights I lie there for quite a while, and other nights I drift off and then wake up very early, around three or four in the morning.

And once I’m awake, my mind starts going. I’ll be thinking about phone calls I need to make, or forms, or whether I handled something the right way, whether I forgot some detail. It’s not even always a clear, useful kind of thinking—it’s more like the same worries circling around when I should be asleep.

By morning I often feel as if I barely rested, even if technically I was in bed for plenty of hours. It’s frustrating, because I’ll think, “Surely tonight I’ll sleep,” and then the same thing happens again.
Before these last eight months, was there ever a time in your life when you felt this same kind of depression nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I don’t think I can say that, no—not with any certainty. I mean, I’ve had periods in my life where I was sad, or worn down, or not myself for a while, like anyone does by this age. But when you ask whether it was this same kind of depression, nearly every day, for at least two weeks… I can’t really identify a time before these last eight months that clearly fits that.

I keep trying to search my memory, and some things blur together. There were hard times, certainly, but I don’t remember it being like this in the same steady, day-after-day way. So I suppose the most honest answer is that I’m not aware of a previous episode like this. If there was one, it isn’t something I can point to and describe confidently.
During these past eight months, have you noticed a change in your appetite?

I’m not really sure that I’ve noticed a clear change, to be honest. I mean, my eating probably varies a bit from day to day, like it always has, but I can’t say there’s been some obvious pattern where I’m much hungrier or not hungry at all.

Sometimes I’ll think, “Did I eat properly today?” but that may just be because I’m paying more attention now that you’re asking. I haven’t been tracking it carefully or anything. So… no, I don’t think there’s been a major appetite change that stands out to me.
During this period, have you been feeling worthless?

Yes… I suppose I have, though I don’t always use that exact word in my head. It’s more that I keep coming back to my brother and how he declined, and I go over it again and again, like I’m reviewing evidence against myself.

I’ll think, if I had been a better sister, if I’d been paying closer attention, if I had called more, asked different questions, noticed something sooner… maybe I could have prevented some of what happened, or at least kept it from getting as bad as it did. And I know, part of me knows, that I may be expecting too much of myself looking back on it now, but it doesn’t really stop the feeling. It’s like I should have known. I should have seen it.

So yes, I’ve felt… not worthless exactly every minute, but guilty, inadequate, like I failed him in some important way. And that feeling has been very hard to set down.
During these past eight months, have you felt noticeably slowed down in your movements or speech?

I don’t think so… not in a way I’ve noticed, anyway. I mean, I’ve had days where I move more slowly just because I’m tired or not especially motivated, but I wouldn’t say people have been telling me I’m speaking slowly, or that I feel like I’m physically moving through molasses or anything like that.

Sometimes I do pause more when I’m trying to answer something, because I’m thinking it through or second-guessing how to say it, but I don’t know if that’s the same thing you mean. As far as walking around, doing ordinary movements, talking with people… I haven’t really noticed a clear, noticeable slowing.
Do you feel depressed even at times when you’re not thinking about your brother or what happened with him?

Yes… I think I do. It isn’t only when I’m actively thinking about my brother, though of course that can make it worse or bring it into sharper focus.

But even at ordinary times, when nothing in particular is happening, I notice it. Like I’ll be making tea in the kitchen, or just standing by the window looking out at the garden, and everything is technically the same as it always was — the kettle, the trees, the light outside — but it all feels muted somehow. Almost as if a gray film has settled over everything. Not dramatic every second, not sobbing all the time, but this quiet heaviness sitting inside me.

And I try to reason with it sometimes. I’ll think, “There’s nothing wrong in this exact moment, you’re just having tea, the garden is there, the day is going on.” But it doesn’t really lift just because I tell myself that. It’s more like the sadness is already there in the background most days, and then thoughts about him attach to it, rather than it only existing because I’m thinking about him.
Do you feel your sadness has lasted longer than you would normally expect after what happened with your brother?

Yes… I think it has. I keep trying to compare it to what seems “reasonable,” though I don’t really know what the right measure is for something like this. But it’s been about eight months now, really since my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly, and the sadness has just… stayed with me.

At first I thought, well, of course I’m upset, anyone would be. It was such a shock, and I kept telling myself it would settle once I had time to absorb it. But month after month, it hasn’t really moved in the way I expected. It doesn’t feel like just the immediate reaction anymore. It feels as if it took root.

So yes, I’d say it has lasted longer than I would have imagined. I don’t know what’s normal, exactly, but eight months feels like a long time to still be carrying it this heavily.
During these past eight months, have you had trouble concentrating?

I’m not sure I’d call it “trouble concentrating” in a clear way. I mean… I can still follow a conversation, and if I’m reading something simple or doing ordinary things around the house, I’m not completely unable to focus.

There are moments where my mind wanders, but I don’t know whether that’s concentration exactly or just me being preoccupied. Sometimes I’ll read the same paragraph again because I realize I wasn’t really taking it in, but that’s happened to me at other times in life too, so I hesitate to make too much of it.

So I’d say… maybe a little at times, but not in a pronounced way that I’ve really noticed as a major problem over these eight months.
If your brother’s situation had not happened, do you think you would still have become this depressed?

I honestly don’t know. I’ve thought about that quite a lot, and I go back and forth with it.

Part of me feels like, no, I wouldn’t have felt this low if all of that with my brother hadn’t happened, because it really did seem to start around then, or at least become much more noticeable around then. It was such a disturbance in the family and in my sense of things being stable. So it’s hard not to connect the two.

But then another part of me wonders whether maybe something in me was already more vulnerable than I realized, and his situation was what brought it out. I can’t really separate it cleanly. I don’t have some parallel version of myself where it didn’t happen, you know? I only know what actually happened, and after that, my mood changed in a way I haven’t been able to shake.

So… my best answer is that I’m not sure. I suspect I wouldn’t have become this depressed without it, but I can’t say that with certainty.
During these past eight months, have you been feeling unusually tired or low in energy?

I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, at my age I suppose there are days when I feel a bit slower or less energetic than I used to, but I haven’t especially noticed some dramatic tiredness that stands out from everything else.

I do have days when I don’t feel very lively, if that makes sense, but I’m not sure whether I’d call it “unusually tired.” Sometimes it feels more like heaviness in my mood than actual physical exhaustion. I can still get through the ordinary parts of the day, even if I’m not exactly bursting with energy.

So… I don’t think tiredness or low energy has been the main thing I’ve been aware of. If it’s there, it’s not something I’ve clearly identified as a separate problem.
During these past eight months, have you found yourself crying much more than usual?

I wouldn’t say I’ve been crying much more, exactly. That’s not really how it has shown itself for me, at least not in some obvious way where I’m breaking down all the time.

It’s more that most days there’s this… grayness over everything. Almost like a film has settled over the day before I’ve even begun it. I can be doing something very ordinary, like making tea, or standing at the window looking out at the garden, and there’s this quiet heaviness inside me. Not necessarily tears, but a kind of sadness that just sits there. And I can tell myself, “Well, nothing is happening right this second,” or try to reason my way out of it, but it doesn’t really lift just because I explain it to myself.

So, crying more than usual—no, not especially. But feeling low in that steady, muted way, yes, very much.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I can say that, no—not with any certainty. I mean, I’ve had periods in my life where I was sad, or worn down, or not myself for a while, like anyone does by this age. But when you ask whether it was this same kind of depression, nearly every day, for at least two weeks… I can’t really identify a time before these last eight months that clearly fits that.

I keep trying to search my memory, and some things blur together. There were hard times, certainly, but I don’t remember it being like this in the same steady, day-after-day way. So I suppose the most honest answer is that I’m not aware of a previous episode like this. If there was one, it isn’t something I can point to and describe confidently.

inference.note: No clear prior depressive episode is identifiable, making recurrent depression (F33.9) less likely. Eight months of depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, passive death wishes, and functional impairment support a current depressive episode (F32.9), though a stress-related disorder (F43.9) remains possible given onset after the brother’s sudden health/behavior change.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive syndrome includes appetite disturbance, which would help support a major depressive episode over a nonspecific stress reaction.
doctor.question: During these past eight months, have you noticed a change in your appetite?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about appetite change, but the provided symptom profile does not include an appetite or weight-change item.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure that I’ve noticed a clear change, to be honest. I mean, my eating probably varies a bit from day to day, like it always has, but I can’t say there’s been some obvious pattern where I’m much hungrier or not hungry at all.

Sometimes I’ll think, “Did I eat properly today?” but that may just be because I’m paying more attention now that you’re asking. I haven’t been tracking it carefully or anything. So… no, I don’t think there’s been a major appetite change that stands out to me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are better characterized as grief focused on the brother or as a broader depressive episode by assessing pervasive worthlessness.
doctor.question: During this period, have you been feeling worthless?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep going back over my brother’s decline and telling myself that if I had been a better sister, or more attentive, I would have noticed sooner and prevented some of this.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feeling worthless during this depressive period, which matches the Worthlessness_Guilt symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yes… I suppose I have, though I don’t always use that exact word in my head. It’s more that I keep coming back to my brother and how he declined, and I go over it again and again, like I’m reviewing evidence against myself.

I’ll think, if I had been a better sister, if I’d been paying closer attention, if I had called more, asked different questions, noticed something sooner… maybe I could have prevented some of what happened, or at least kept it from getting as bad as it did. And I know, part of me knows, that I may be expecting too much of myself looking back on it now, but it doesn’t really stop the feeling. It’s like I should have known. I should have seen it.

So yes, I’ve felt… not worthless exactly every minute, but guilty, inadequate, like I failed him in some important way. And that feeling has been very hard to set down.

doctor.intent: Differentiate major depressive disorder from a stress-related disorder by checking for psychomotor change, which would support a major depressive episode if present.
doctor.question: During these past eight months, have you felt noticeably slowed down in your movements or speech?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about psychomotor slowing in movement or speech, which is not covered by any item in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in a way I’ve noticed, anyway. I mean, I’ve had days where I move more slowly just because I’m tired or not especially motivated, but I wouldn’t say people have been telling me I’m speaking slowly, or that I feel like I’m physically moving through molasses or anything like that.

Sometimes I do pause more when I’m trying to answer something, because I’m thinking it through or second-guessing how to say it, but I don’t know if that’s the same thing you mean. As far as walking around, doing ordinary movements, talking with people… I haven’t really noticed a clear, noticeable slowing.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are pervasive rather than primarily tied to the stressor, helping distinguish a major depressive episode from a stress-related adjustment reaction.
doctor.question: Do you feel depressed even at times when you’re not thinking about your brother or what happened with him?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I feel as if a gray film has settled over everything, and even when I’m making tea or looking out at my garden, there’s this quiet heaviness in me that I can’t quite reason my way out of.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether a depressed mood is present generally, even when not focused on guilt or thoughts about her brother.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think I do. It isn’t only when I’m actively thinking about my brother, though of course that can make it worse or bring it into sharper focus.

But even at ordinary times, when nothing in particular is happening, I notice it. Like I’ll be making tea in the kitchen, or just standing by the window looking out at the garden, and everything is technically the same as it always was — the kettle, the trees, the light outside — but it all feels muted somehow. Almost as if a gray film has settled over everything. Not dramatic every second, not sobbing all the time, but this quiet heaviness sitting inside me.

And I try to reason with it sometimes. I’ll think, “There’s nothing wrong in this exact moment, you’re just having tea, the garden is there, the day is going on.” But it doesn’t really lift just because I tell myself that. It’s more like the sadness is already there in the background most days, and then thoughts about him attach to it, rather than it only existing because I’m thinking about him.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are occurring in excess of what would be expected from an identifiable stressor, helping distinguish major depressive disorder from an unspecified stress-related disorder.
doctor.question: Do you feel your sadness has lasted longer than you would normally expect after what happened with your brother?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about eight months, since my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the sadness has persisted longer than expected, which directly concerns the duration of the symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think it has. I keep trying to compare it to what seems “reasonable,” though I don’t really know what the right measure is for something like this. But it’s been about eight months now, really since my brother’s health and behavior changed so suddenly, and the sadness has just… stayed with me.

At first I thought, well, of course I’m upset, anyone would be. It was such a shock, and I kept telling myself it would settle once I had time to absorb it. But month after month, it hasn’t really moved in the way I expected. It doesn’t feel like just the immediate reaction anymore. It feels as if it took root.

So yes, I’d say it has lasted longer than I would have imagined. I don’t know what’s normal, exactly, but eight months feels like a long time to still be carrying it this heavily.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive syndrome includes impaired concentration, which would support a major depressive episode over an unspecified stress-related disorder.
doctor.question: During these past eight months, have you had trouble concentrating?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about trouble concentrating, but the provided symptom profile does not include a concentration or indecisiveness symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call it “trouble concentrating” in a clear way. I mean… I can still follow a conversation, and if I’m reading something simple or doing ordinary things around the house, I’m not completely unable to focus.

There are moments where my mind wanders, but I don’t know whether that’s concentration exactly or just me being preoccupied. Sometimes I’ll read the same paragraph again because I realize I wasn’t really taking it in, but that’s happened to me at other times in life too, so I hesitate to make too much of it.

So I’d say… maybe a little at times, but not in a pronounced way that I’ve really noticed as a major problem over these eight months.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are closely tied to the identifiable stressor and would be expected as an adjustment reaction, versus occurring independently as a major depressive episode.
doctor.question: If your brother’s situation had not happened, do you think you would still have become this depressed?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about the cause or trigger of the depression—whether it would have occurred without the brother’s situation—which is not a specific symptom item in the provided profile.

patient.answer:
I honestly don’t know. I’ve thought about that quite a lot, and I go back and forth with it.

Part of me feels like, no, I wouldn’t have felt this low if all of that with my brother hadn’t happened, because it really did seem to start around then, or at least become much more noticeable around then. It was such a disturbance in the family and in my sense of things being stable. So it’s hard not to connect the two.

But then another part of me wonders whether maybe something in me was already more vulnerable than I realized, and his situation was what brought it out. I can’t really separate it cleanly. I don’t have some parallel version of myself where it didn’t happen, you know? I only know what actually happened, and after that, my mood changed in a way I haven’t been able to shake.

So… my best answer is that I’m not sure. I suspect I wouldn’t have become this depressed without it, but I can’t say that with certainty.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a depressive episode from a stress-related adjustment reaction by checking for low energy, which would add another core vegetative depressive symptom and strengthen F32.9.
doctor.question: During these past eight months, have you been feeling unusually tired or low in energy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fatigue or low energy, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific item for fatigue or loss of energy.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, at my age I suppose there are days when I feel a bit slower or less energetic than I used to, but I haven’t especially noticed some dramatic tiredness that stands out from everything else.

I do have days when I don’t feel very lively, if that makes sense, but I’m not sure whether I’d call it “unusually tired.” Sometimes it feels more like heaviness in my mood than actual physical exhaustion. I can still get through the ordinary parts of the day, even if I’m not exactly bursting with energy.

So… I don’t think tiredness or low energy has been the main thing I’ve been aware of. If it’s there, it’s not something I’ve clearly identified as a separate problem.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a depressive episode from a stress-related adjustment disorder by determining whether the patient has had recurrent crying spells, which would add another major depressive symptom and strengthen F32.9 over F43.9.
doctor.question: During these past eight months, have you found yourself crying much more than usual?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I feel as if a gray film has settled over everything, and even when I’m making tea or looking out at my garden, there’s this quiet heaviness in me that I can’t quite reason my way out of.
target_item.reason: Crying much more than usual is most directly related to persistent sadness or depressed mood.

patient.answer:
I wouldn’t say I’ve been crying much more, exactly. That’s not really how it has shown itself for me, at least not in some obvious way where I’m breaking down all the time.

It’s more that most days there’s this… grayness over everything. Almost like a film has settled over the day before I’ve even begun it. I can be doing something very ordinary, like making tea, or standing at the window looking out at the garden, and there’s this quiet heaviness inside me. Not necessarily tears, but a kind of sadness that just sits there. And I can tell myself, “Well, nothing is happening right this second,” or try to reason my way out of it, but it doesn’t really lift just because I explain it to myself.

So, crying more than usual—no, not especially. But feeling low in that steady, muted way, yes, very much.
